title: Monolayer MoS2 as a Window Material for High-Resolution Liquid-Phase Electron Microscopy and Spectroscopy
content: Liquid-phase electron microscopy enables direct imaging and real-time investigation of physical, chemical, and biological processes in their native liquid environments, offering new insights into dynamic material transformations at the nanoscale. Traditional silicon nitride liquid cells (LCs) suffer from thick windows, excessive liquid layers, and electron beam-induced radiolysis, limiting resolution. The realization of graphene liquid cells (GLCs) a decade ago mitigated these challenges by encapsulating liquid between two graphene layers, forming ultrathin, stable pockets that sustain high vacuum conditions, enabling the study of dynamics processes in liquid phase [1,2]. This advancement significantly improved imaging and spectroscopy capabilities, particularly by enabling high-resolution studies with controlled electron dose rates [3,4]. Further developments introduced hexagonal boron nitride liquid cells (BNLCs), which enhance low-energy electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) and enable vibrational spectroscopy [5]. However, challenges such as beam-induced damage and bubble formation persist, necessitating alternative window materials.
